title: Let My People Go
subtitle: Exodus in Poems & Pictures
beforeYouBegin:
Exodus runs from brick kilns in Egypt to a tent in the desert with God living in the middle of the camp: a basket in the reeds, a burning bush, a marked doorway, a road through the sea, bread from the sky, a mountain on fire.

This book walks through it in forty short poems, in four parts. Each poem sits beside a picture and under a single line of Scripture. It doesn't cover every chapter; it stops at the moments that carry the story.

The poems are not the Bible. They are one reader's response to it. Open Exodus alongside this book, and let the real words have the last word.

parts.title: Part One · Out of the Reeds
parts.epigraph: God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant

parts.title: Part Two · Let My People Go
parts.epigraph: Let my people go, that they may serve me.

parts.title: Part Three · Through the Sea
parts.epigraph: Yahweh will fight for you, and you shall be still.

parts.title: Part Four · The Mountain and the Tent

paintings.title: the midwives
paintings.poem:
the first heroes of Exodus
aren't famous.
Shiphrah and Puah,
two midwives.
the king of Egypt said:
kill the boys.
they went back to work
and delivered them.
before the plagues,
before the sea,
the rescue began
with two women
who feared God
more than Pharaoh.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: History forgot the title of that Pharaoh, yet heaven remembered the names of Shiphrah and Puah: where is God asking for quiet, uncelebrated courage in your corner of the world?

paintings.title: the basket
paintings.poem:
when she couldn't hide him any longer,
she did the only thing left:
she wove a basket,
sealed it tight,
and let go.
the same word as Noah's ark—
a little ark,
floating on the river
that was meant to drown him.
sometimes faith
looks like a mother's hands
opening.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Jochebed wove a reed basket and let the current take what she could no longer hide: what person or worry do you need to move from your clenched grip into the hands of God today?

paintings.title: drawn out
paintings.poem:
Pharaoh's own daughter
found him crying in the reeds,
and pitied him.
and the baby's sister
stepped out of hiding:
shall I find you a nurse?
so his mother
was paid
to raise her own son.
she named him Moses—
drawn out.
a whole nation
would one day be drawn out
behind him.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If you were walking this road with a close friend and stopped at “drawn out” (Exodus 2:5-10), what would you talk about after reading, “a whole nation would one day be drawn out behind him”?

paintings.title: it went up
paintings.poem:
the years went by.
the king died.
the bricks did not stop.
and they groaned,
and cried,
and it went up.
God heard.
God remembered.
God saw.
and he cared.
no cry of yours
has ever stopped
at the ceiling.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Pause before the quiet centerpiece of “it went up”: what changes in your posture today when you sit with the closing words of “it went up”—“no cry of yours has ever stopped at the ceiling”?

paintings.title: turn aside
paintings.poem:
eighty years old,
a shepherd now,
far from the palace—
and a bush onfire
that wouldn't burn up.
he turned aside to look.
that's all it took:
curiosity,
a detour,
a man willing to stop
and see.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The bush burned in the scrubland, yet God waited to speak until Moses turned aside to look: what small wonder along your ordinary path will you miss today if you don’t slow your pace?

paintings.title: holy ground
paintings.poem:
take off  your sandals.
the same dirt he'd walked for years
with sheep.
the same rocks.
holy ground.
God doesn't only meet us
in temples.
he turns ordinary ground
holy
by showing up on it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In Exodus 3:4-5, the story turns on the dust on your sandals—and ends with, “he turns ordinary ground holy by showing up on it.” What small, unhurried faithfulness is God inviting you into today?

paintings.title: who am I?
paintings.poem:
who am I? he asked.
a fair question.
a fugitive. a shepherd.
a man who ran from Egypt
long ago.
and God didn't answer it.
he didn't say:
you are strong,
you are ready,
you are enough.
he said:
I will be with you.
the answer
to a better question.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The world measures life by speed and noise, yet Exodus 3:11-12 points us to the quiet centerpiece of “who am I?” and whispers, “the answer to a better question.” How can you practice that unhurried wisdom today?

paintings.title: I AM
paintings.poem:
what's your name? Moses asked.
they'll want to know.
and God gave a name
that is also a sentence:
I am who I am.
not a title.
not a job.
being itself,
speaking.
you don't need to know
what I'll do, he seemed to say.
you need to know
I am.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The poem closes with a quiet turn: “being itself, speaking. you need to know I am.” Where in your life right now does that line hit closest to home?

paintings.title: in your hand
paintings.poem:
what's in your hand?
a stick.
a shepherd's rod.
nothing special.
God said: throw it down.
and then: pick it up.
that stick
would one day split a sea.
God rarely asks
for what you don't have.
he asks
for what's already in your hand.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Sometimes a single sentence opens a window in a closed room: how does “he asks for what's already in your hand” (Exodus 4:1-5) speak to a question you have been carrying lately?

paintings.title: no straw
paintings.poem:
Moses asked for freedom,
and things got worse.
no more straw.
same number of bricks.
sometimes obedience
is followed by a harder week,
not a better one.
the story isn't over
in chapterfive.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Hold your hands open for a moment before “no straw” (Exodus 5:6-9): what are you gripping tightly that loosens when you hear, “the story isn't over in chapterfive”?

paintings.title: the river
paintings.poem:
Egypt trusted the Nile.
it fed them,
watered them—
and had drowned the Hebrew boys.
so the first sign
struck the river.
the thing they trusted most
turned against them.
every plague that followed
asked the same question:
which god
is really God?
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Scripture remembers this moment in Exodus 7:19-21 not to impress us, but to steady us: when have you seen the truth that “every plague that followed asked the same question: which god is really God?” in your own story?

paintings.title: tomorrow
paintings.poem:
frogs in the ovens.
frogs in the beds.
frogs in the king's own room.
when do you want them gone?
Moses asked.
and Pharaoh said:
tomorrow.
one more night with the frogs.
how often
do we choose that—
one more night
with the thing we're begging God
to take away?
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As your pilgrim lantern pauses at “tomorrow” (Exodus 8:8-10), what one honest sentence would you pray beside the quiet centerpiece of “tomorrow” after reading, “how often do we choose that— one more night with the thing we're begging God to take away?”?

paintings.title: light in Goshen
paintings.poem:
darkness so thick
you could feel it.
three days.
no one moved.
and in Goshen,
in the slaves' houses,
light.
the same land.
the same night.
a diff erent house.
the dark was real.
so was the light
in the homes
that belonged to him.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Between the opening line (“darkness so thick you could feel it”) and the closing thought (“so was the light in the homes that belonged to him”), what is Exodus 10:21-23 gently reframing in your own day?

paintings.title: when I see
paintings.poem:
a lamb for each house.
its blood on the doorframe.
hyssop in the hand.
not because God needed a sign
tofind them.
because they needed one
to know
where to stand.
when I see the blood,
I will pass over you.
Christians have been reading
that line
ever since.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Along the road of Let My People Go, “when I see” (Exodus 12:7-13) slows us down at your own two hands to remind us: “Christians have been reading that line ever since.” Where are you being invited to trade control for trust today?

paintings.title: in haste
paintings.poem:
eat it standing up.
belt fastened.
sandals on.
staff  in hand.
this isn't a meal
for lingering.
it's the last supper
of slaves
and the first breakfast
of free people.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If you were walking this road with a close friend and stopped at “in haste” (Exodus 12:8-11), what would you talk about after reading, “it's the last supper of slaves and the first breakfast of free people”?

paintings.title: no time to rise
paintings.poem:
no time for the bread to rise.
they tied the dough in their cloaks,
kneading bowls and all,
and walked out of Egypt
with breakfast on their shoulders.
freedom came so fast
the bread
couldn't keep up.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Pause before the daily loaf broken in the hand: what changes in your posture today when you sit with the closing words of “no time to rise”—“freedom came so fast the bread couldn't keep up”?

paintings.title: remember
paintings.poem:
remember.
because you will forget.
the cracked hands.
the bricks.
the cry that went up.
remembering
isn't looking backward.
it's how you stay free.
every year, at the same table,
tell it again.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look at the stillness of the table set before you in Timothy’s painting: what striving can you lay down as you ponder, “every year, at the same table, tell it again” (Exodus 13:3)?

paintings.title: the pillar
paintings.poem:
by day, a cloud.
by night, fire.
they never had a map.
they had a presence
that moved.
when it went, they went.
when it stopped, they stopped.
it's a strange way to travel.
it's how he has led
his people
ever since.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In Exodus 13:21-22, the story turns on the warmth of the fire—and ends with, “it's how he has led his people ever since.” What small, unhurried faithfulness is God inviting you into today?

paintings.title: stand still
paintings.poem:
the sea in front.
the army behind.
nowhere to go.
and Moses said:
don't be afraid.
stand still.
the Lord will fight for you.
sometimes faith
is doing nothing—
not out of fear,
but out of trust
that someone else
is about to move.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The world measures life by speed and noise, yet Exodus 14:10-14 points us to the quiet centerpiece of “stand still” and whispers, “sometimes faith is doing nothing— not out of fear, but out of trust that someone else is about to move.” How can you practice that unhurried wisdom today?

paintings.title: a road through
paintings.poem:
all night
an east wind blew.
and in the morning,
a road
where the sea had been.
walls of water
on the right
and on the left,
and a whole people
walking through
on dry ground.
he doesn't always
take away the sea.
sometimes
he makes a road through it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The poem closes with a quiet turn: “sometimes he makes a road through it.” Where in your life right now does that line hit closest to home?

paintings.title: wet feet
paintings.poem:
first the silence of the crossing,
then the far shore,
then Miriam
picking up a tambourine.
and every woman followed her,
dancing on the sand.
sing to the Lord,
she called—
and a song
was born
with wet feet.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Sometimes a single sentence opens a window in a closed room: how does “sing to the Lord, she called— and a song was born with wet feet” (Exodus 15:20-21) speak to a question you have been carrying lately?

paintings.title: bitter water
paintings.poem:
three days after the miracle
they were thirsty,
and the water was bitter.
it didn't take long
to forget the sea.
and God didn't scold.
he showed Moses a tree,
and the tree went into the water,
and the water turned sweet.
he is patient
with short memories.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Hold your hands open for a moment before “bitter water” (Exodus 15:22-25): what are you gripping tightly that loosens when you hear, “he is patient with short memories”?

paintings.title: what is it?
paintings.poem:
the name of the bread
is a question:
what is it?
flakes like frost on the ground
every morning
for forty years.
they never could explain it.
they could only
gather it
and give thanks.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Scripture remembers this moment in Exodus 16:13-15 not to impress us, but to steady us: when have you seen the truth that “they could only gather it and give thanks” in your own story?

paintings.title: enough
paintings.poem:
some gathered a lot.
some gathered a little.
and when they measured it,
everyone had enough.
no one hoarding.
no one hungry.
it was bread.
it was also a lesson
in how God's economy
works.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As your pilgrim lantern pauses at “enough” (Exodus 16:16-18), what one honest sentence would you pray beside the daily loaf broken in the hand after reading, “it was also a lesson in how God's economy works”?

paintings.title: water from stone
paintings.poem:
they argued.
they tested.
they nearly stoned him.
and God said:
I'll stand there on the rock.
strike it.
water from stone.
when we are at our most unreasonable,
he is still
bringing water
out of the hardest place.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Between the opening line (“they argued. they tested”) and the closing thought (“when we are at our most unreasonable, he is still bringing water out of the hardest place”), what is Exodus 17:3-6 gently reframing in your own day?

paintings.title: held-up hands
paintings.poem:
the battle went well
while his hands were raised,
and badly
when they dropped.
and his arms got tired.
so they sat him on a stone,
and two friends
held up his hands,
one on each side,
until the sun went down.
nobody can hold on
all day alone.
find your Aaron.
find your Hur.
be one.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Along the road of Let My People Go, “held-up hands” (Exodus 17:11-12) slows us down at the stone well in the heat of the day to remind us: “find your Aaron. find your Hur. be one.” Where are you being invited to trade control for trust today?

paintings.title: too heavy
paintings.poem:
morning to evening,
Moses settled every dispute
himself.
his father-in-law watched
and said:
this isn't good.
you'll wear out.
you can't do this alone.
sometimes the wisest advice
comes from your in-laws:
get help.
share the load.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If you were walking this road with a close friend and stopped at “too heavy” (Exodus 18:13-18), what would you talk about after reading, “sometimes the wisest advice comes from your in-laws: get help. share the load”?

paintings.title: eagles' wings
paintings.poem:
before the rules,
a reminder:
you saw what I did.
I carried you
on eagles' wings.
I brought you
to myself.
not to a place.
not to a law.
to me.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Pause before the quiet centerpiece of “eagles' wings”: what changes in your posture today when you sit with the closing words of “eagles' wings”—“not to a place. not to a law. to me”?

paintings.title: the mountain smoked
paintings.poem:
thunder. lightning.
a trumpet growing louder.
the whole mountain shaking.
this is not a tame God.
and yet—
he came down.
to them.
to talk.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look at the stillness of the clear note of the horn in Timothy’s painting: what striving can you lay down as you ponder, “and yet— he came down. to them. to talk” (Exodus 19:16-18)?

paintings.title: who brought you out
paintings.poem:
the commandments begin
not with a command
but with a rescue:
I am the one who brought you out.
first he saves them.
then he tells them
how free people live.
the law isn't the ladder
out of Egypt.
it's the shape of life
after.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In Exodus 20:1-3, the story turns on the stone pillow at Bethel—and ends with, “it's the shape of life after.” What small, unhurried faithfulness is God inviting you into today?

paintings.title: a day off
paintings.poem:
slaves never get a day off .
so one of the first things God gives
freed slaves,
built right into the law,
is rest.
one day in seven
to remember:
you are not bricks.
you are not Pharaoh's.
you are his.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The world measures life by speed and noise, yet Exodus 20:8-11 points us to the quiet centerpiece of “a day off” and whispers, “you are not Pharaoh's. you are his.” How can you practice that unhurried wisdom today?

paintings.title: thick darkness
paintings.poem:
the people stood far off .
Moses went closer—
into the thick darkness,
where God was.
we expect tofind him
in the light.
sometimes he is waiting
in the part
we can't see through.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The poem closes with a quiet turn: “sometimes he is waiting in the part we can't see through.” Where in your life right now does that line hit closest to home?

paintings.title: the calf
paintings.poem:
forty days is a long time
to wait for a man on a mountain.
so they took off  their earrings
and made a god
they could see,
and said:
this is the one who saved you.
it was a calf.
it couldn't save anything.
we still do it—
melt down what God gave us
into something smaller
we can hold.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Sometimes a single sentence opens a window in a closed room: how does “we still do it— melt down what God gave us into something smaller we can hold” (Exodus 32:1-4) speak to a question you have been carrying lately?

paintings.title: blot me out
paintings.poem:
forgive them, Moses prayed.
and if you won't—
blot me out of your book instead.
he'd rather lose his own place
than lose them.
it wouldn't be the last time
someone stood
between God's people
and what they deserved,
and off ered himself.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Hold your hands open for a moment before “blot me out” (Exodus 32:30-32): what are you gripping tightly that loosens when you hear, “it wouldn't be the last time someone stood between God's people and what they deserved, and off ered himself”?

paintings.title: as a friend
paintings.poem:
not as a king to a servant.
not as a judge to the accused.
as a man
speaks to his friend.
that was the tent's secret:
the God of the smoking mountain
wanted someone
to talk with.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Scripture remembers this moment in Exodus 33:7-11 not to impress us, but to steady us: when have you seen the truth that “that was the tent's secret: the God of the smoking mountain wanted someone to talk with” in your own story?

paintings.title: the cleft of the rock
paintings.poem:
show me your glory, he asked.
and God said:
no one can see my face and live.
but I'll hide you in the rock,
and cover you with my hand,
and pass by,
and you will see
where I've been.
sometimes that's how we see him:
looking back,
from the cleft,
at the glory
that just went by.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As your pilgrim lantern pauses at “the cleft of the rock” (Exodus 33:18-23), what one honest sentence would you pray beside your own two hands after reading, “sometimes that's how we see him: looking back, from the cleft, at the glory that just went by”?

paintings.title: his name
paintings.poem:
Moses asked to see his glory,
and God answered
with his name:
merciful.
gracious.
slow to anger.
over flowing with love
and faithfulness.
prophets would quote these lines
for centuries—
even Jonah,
complaining.
this is who he said he is,
the morning after the calf.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Between the opening line (“Moses asked to see his glory, and God answered with his name: merciful”) and the closing thought (“this is who he said he is, the morning after the calf”), what is Exodus 34:5-7 gently reframing in your own day?

paintings.title: shining
paintings.poem:
he came down the mountain
with his face shining,
and didn't know it.
that's the best kind of glow—
the kind you don't notice
you're wearing.
time with God
shows on people
before they know it does.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Along the road of Let My People Go, “shining” (Exodus 34:29-35) slows us down at the long climb up the hill to remind us: “time with God shows on people before they know it does.” Where are you being invited to trade control for trust today?

paintings.title: more than enough
paintings.poem:
the same people who gave their gold
to make a calf
now gave it
to make a home for God—
so much
that Moses had to say:
stop.
we have more than enough.
imagine a building project
where they had to tell people
to stop giving.
grace does that
to a closed hand.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If you were walking this road with a close friend and stopped at “more than enough” (Exodus 36:3-7), what would you talk about after reading, “grace does that to a closed hand”?

paintings.title: moving in
paintings.poem:
the book began
with slaves making bricks
for Pharaoh's cities.
it ends
with free people
setting up a tent for God—
and God moving in.
cloud by day.
fire by night.
through all their journeys.
he didn't just bring them out.
he came to live
in the middle of the camp.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Pause before the warmth of the fire: what changes in your posture today when you sit with the closing words of “moving in”—“he came to live in the middle of the camp”?
